title: The Story of Money · Episode 1
chapters: Shells, silver and plastic: a history of money
The Medici: the bankers who built a Renaissance
How banks create money out of thin air

units.t: The Story of Money. Episode one.
In this episode: Shells, silver and plastic: a history of money, The Medici: the bankers who built a Renaissance and How banks create money out of thin air.
Part one. Shells, silver and plastic: a history of money.
Money is one of humanity's strangest inventions: a shared story that strangers agree to believe.
Here's how it went from clay tablets to tap and go.
The barter myth.
The textbook story says a baker wants shoes, the shoemaker wants fish, and nobody can trade until someone invents money.
It has been told since Adam Smith's day.
But anthropologists have struggled to find any society that ran on everyday barter.
In small communities, people shared, gave gifts and kept informal track of who owed whom.
Barter mostly showed up between strangers, or where money had collapsed, such as prisoner of war camps where cigarettes became currency.
David Graeber made the argument famous in his 2011 book Debt: The First 5,000 Years.
Credit and obligation probably came before coins, not after.
Money began as a way of keeping score.
Debts in clay.
More than 4,000 years ago in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, scribes pressed marks into wet clay to record who owed what.
Temples and palaces collected grain, managed workers and lent out goods, so they needed a common yardstick.
They settled on weights of silver, measured in shekels, alongside measures of barley.
A farmer might owe a debt valued in silver but pay it in grain at harvest, while the silver stayed locked in the temple.
One of money's oldest jobs is as a unit of account.
Paying with a physical object came later.
Shells, stones and coins.
People have used remarkable things as money.
Cowrie shells circulated for centuries across parts of Africa and Asia because they were durable, hard to fake and easy to count.
On the island of Yap, people used huge carved stone discs called rai, some too heavy to move, so ownership changed by community agreement while the stone stayed put.
The first stamped coins appeared in Lydia, in what is now western Turkey, around the 600s BC.
Made of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver, they were stamped by the state to vouch for their weight.
A ruler's stamp turned a lump of metal into something people could trust without weighing it.
Paper and punched coins.
Heavy iron and copper coins were a nuisance, so merchants in Sichuan, China, began depositing coins for paper receipts.
In the Song dynasty, around the early 1000s, the government issued official paper money.
In Europe, paper money grew out of goldsmiths and banks writing receipts for gold deposits, which were passed around as payment.
It works only if people believe it can be spent, and Chinese dynasties learned that printing too many notes made them lose value.
The paper wasn't valuable; the promise was.
In colonial New South Wales, coins were so scarce that rum acted like a currency.
In 1813 Governor Macquarie had a hole punched out of Spanish silver dollars, making two coins, the holey dollar and the dump, which stayed in the colony.
Australia went decimal in February 1966.
Gold, faith and data.
By the late 1800s many leading economies were on the gold standard, with paper money swappable for a fixed amount of gold.
After the Second World War, currencies were linked to the US dollar, which was convertible to gold, until President Nixon ended that in 1971.
Since then most money has been fiat: valued because governments declare it legal tender, accept it for taxes, and central banks try to keep it stable.
Australia issued the world's first polymer banknote in 1988.
Yet cash is shrinking as people tap cards and phones, and most money is now numbers in accounts.
Bitcoin, launched in 2009, tried to work without a central issuer, though its price swings wildly.
Money works because enough people agree that it does.
The key idea: Money probably began as a way of keeping score of debts, not as a fix for awkward barter.
Part two. The Medici: the bankers who built a Renaissance.
A family of Florentine money-changers became bankers to the Pope, patrons of genius and rulers of a city.
Their tricks still shape finance today.
Men at the bench.
In the 1300s Italian cities such as Florence, Venice and Genoa were the trading hubs of Europe, awash with coins from dozens of states.
Merchants needed someone to weigh, test and swap these coins, and to move money safely over long distances.
Money-changers set up at tables, and the Italian word for such a bench, banco, gave us the word bank.
A banker who could not pay was said to be banca rotta, a broken bench, the root of our word bankrupt.
In 1397 Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici founded the Medici Bank in Florence.
Within a few decades it would become the most powerful bank in Europe.
God's banker.
The Medici's greatest client was the papacy.
The Church collected revenue from England to Poland and needed to move it to Rome without carting silver across the Alps.
The Medici's network of trusted agents could do it, and for long stretches of the 1400s they were the Pope's main bankers.
Later family members became popes, including Leo X and Clement VII.
There was an awkward problem.
The Church condemned usury, meaning interest on a loan.
The answer was the bill of exchange.
A Florentine merchant handed over florins and received a document payable months later in another currency, say in Bruges or London.
The rates were set so the banker profited, but on paper it was a currency exchange, not a loan.
In practice, interest was hidden inside the exchange.
A multinational company.
At its height the Medici Bank had branches in Rome, Venice, Milan, Geneva, Avignon, Bruges and London, among other places.
Each was run by a manager who often held a share of the profits, giving him a reason to work hard, while the family in Florence kept overall control.
Branches were set up as separate partnerships, so a disaster in one city would not automatically drag down the rest.
The Medici and other Italian merchants also kept careful accounts using double-entry bookkeeping, recording every transaction as both a debit and a credit so errors stood out.
The method was spreading among Italian traders by the 1300s, and the friar Luca Pacioli described it in print in 1494.
Money, art and power.
Giovanni's son Cosimo de' Medici used the bank's fortune to become the unofficial ruler of Florence from 1434, steering politics through allies rather than holding a crown.
He was also a generous patron.
He funded churches, the library of the monastery of San Marco and artists such as Donatello, and supported scholars who translated ancient Greek philosophy.
His grandson Lorenzo the Magnificent continued the tradition, and the young Michelangelo spent time in his household.
Part of this giving was genuine love of learning and beauty.
Part of it was likely an attempt to win public support, and perhaps to ease consciences troubled by the Church's teaching on wealth.
Either way, Florence was transformed.
The fall of the bank.
Under Lorenzo, who was more interested in politics and poetry than ledgers, the bank weakened.
Some branch managers made reckless loans to princes, who were powerful, unpredictable and hard to sue.
The London branch lent heavily to King Edward IV during the Wars of the Roses and suffered heavy losses.
The Bruges branch, under Tommaso Portinari, lent to Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, who was killed in battle in 1477.
One by one, branches closed.
In 1494, when the Medici were driven out of Florence, the bank collapsed.
The lesson echoes through financial history: lending to the mighty can feel safe until the mighty decide, or are unable, to pay.
The key idea: Banking in Renaissance Italy began with money-changers working at benches in the street.
Part three. How banks create money out of thin air.
When a bank approves a home loan, it doesn't hand over someone else's savings.
It creates brand new money with a few keystrokes.
The loan creates money.
Imagine a couple borrowing $600,000 for a house.
Most people assume the bank passes along other customers' savings.
Not quite.
When the loan is approved, the bank records a loan the couple owes it, and a matching deposit paid to the seller's account.
That deposit didn't exist a moment earlier.
It is brand new money, spendable like any other in a bank account.
The Bank of England explained this in a 2014 article, 'Money creation in the modern economy', and the Reserve Bank of Australia describes it the same way.
Most money in the economy is created like this.
What counts as money.
The balance in your banking app is not cash in a vault with your name on it.
It is a promise from your bank to pay you, an IOU you can use to make payments.
When you tap your card, the bank moves that promise to someone else's account.
These deposits count as part of the money supply, and they dwarf physical cash.
Banknotes are issued by the Reserve Bank, and coins by the federal government and made by the Royal Australian Mint.
But most day to day money is bank deposits, so private banks create most of a modern country's money, under rules set by public authorities.
Textbook versus reality.
Many textbooks describe a money multiplier: savers deposit money, the bank keeps a fraction in reserve and lends the rest, which is deposited and lent again.
It isn't completely wrong, because lending ripples through the system.
But central banks have said it gets cause and effect backwards.
Banks don't usually wait for deposits.
They lend when they find creditworthy borrowers, and the deposits are created in the process.
Afterwards, they manage the consequences, such as holding enough reserves to settle payments with other banks.
So the amount of money depends heavily on how much people and businesses want to borrow.
Created and destroyed.
Repaying a loan does the opposite of taking one.
When the couple makes a mortgage repayment, their deposit and the loan balance both fall, and that money effectively vanishes.
The money supply grows when new lending outpaces repayments and can shrink when people rush to pay down debt, as in some economies after the 2008 financial crisis.
A surge in lending pumps new money into houses, cars and businesses, which can push prices up.
What limits lending?
Banks need borrowers likely to repay, because bad loans cost money.
APRA requires them to hold enough capital and liquid assets.
Funding costs interest.
And when the RBA raises its cash rate, fewer people borrow and less money is created.
It is a powerful but imprecise lever.
When trust breaks.
Banks hold only a small portion of assets as ready cash and reserves.
That's fine, because depositors don't all want their money on the same day.
But if people fear a bank is in trouble, they may rush to withdraw, and the fear becomes self fulfilling.
This is a bank run.
Customers queued outside Northern Rock in Britain in 2007, and in 2023 depositors pulled billions from Silicon Valley Bank in hours, largely through phone apps.
Australia's Financial Claims Scheme protects deposits up to a set limit per person per bank; check the current figure at fcs.
gov.
au.
None of this means banks print free money, since every loan carries risk and must be repaid.
This is general information, not financial advice; see moneysmart.

The key idea: When a bank approves a loan, it creates a new deposit that didn't exist a moment earlier.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What does the evidence suggest about how money began?
Answer. Credit and obligation probably came before coins.
Question two. How did banking begin in Renaissance Italy?
Answer. Money-changers at street tables swapped and moved coins.
Question three. What happens when a bank approves a home loan?
Answer. It records the loan and creates a matching new deposit.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
